title: 5 Best Practices for Protecting Your Digital Assets
summary: Learn five best practices for protecting digital assets, from secure wallets and transaction controls to account security, phishing defense, and scam awareness.
body_markdown:
## Key Takeaways


-


[Cold storage](https://www.bitgo.com/products/custody-wallet/?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=custody&utm_campaign=best_practices_protecting_assets) reduces exposure to online attacks, but protecting digital assets also requires controls over who can access funds and authorize transactions.


-


Strong passwords, multifactor authentication, and updated devices help protect the accounts and systems used to manage cryptocurrency.


-


[Phishing attacks](https://www.cisa.gov/secure-our-world/recognize-and-report-phishing) can steal credentials or trick users into approving malicious transactions, even without exposing their private keys.


-


Scammers can impersonate trusted organizations through phone calls, messages, and[AI-generated voices](https://www.bitgo.com/resources/blog/guarding-against-social-engineering-attacks/?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=custody&utm_campaign=best_practices_protecting_assets) . Unexpected requests involving sensitive information or asset transfers should always be independently verified.


-


Fraudulent investment opportunities often rely on unrealistic returns, fabricated trading results, and pressure to act quickly. Researching platforms and verifying claims before transferring funds can help prevent losses.


Cryptocurrency security has faced a series of major setbacks in 2026, exposing vulnerabilities across exchanges, hardware wallets, and the systems used to safeguard digital assets. The most significant incident came in October, when[Binance reported a security breach](https://www.binance.com/en/support/announcement/detail/c5a8729a97ac486d963784d96c5642d7) affecting an estimated $6.3 billion in assets, potentially making it the largest cryptocurrency hack on record.


Individual holders have also faced serious threats. A[Coldcard firmware vulnerability](https://bitcoinmagazine.com/news/coldcard-security-risk-immediate-action-required) weakened the generation of wallet recovery seeds, allowing attackers to reconstruct private keys and steal funds. Meanwhile, a[Ledger hardware tampering attack](https://www.ledger.com/blog-response-hardware-implant-attack) targeted devices distributed through certain third-party resellers, exposing recovery phrases during wallet setup.


These incidents demonstrate that protecting digital assets requires more than keeping private keys offline. Attackers can exploit software vulnerabilities, compromise transaction systems, tamper with hardware, steal account credentials, or deceive users into authorizing fraudulent transfers. With cryptocurrency transactions generally irreversible, recovering stolen assets can be extremely difficult.


The following five best practices can help reduce these risks, from securing wallets and accounts to controlling transactions and recognizing scams.


## 1. Protect Your Assets With Secure Wallets and Transaction Controls


Hot wallets are connected to the internet, making them convenient for trading, payments, and other frequent transactions. That connectivity also exposes them to risks involving compromised devices, stolen credentials, and attacks against connected systems.


Cold wallets keep private keys offline, reducing exposure to internet-based attacks. They are generally better suited for assets that do not need to be accessed frequently. Many holders balance security and accessibility by keeping smaller amounts in hot wallets while storing the majority of their assets in[cold storage](https://www.bitgo.com/products/custody-wallet/?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=custody&utm_campaign=best_practices_protecting_assets) .


Cold storage does not eliminate every security risk. Even when private keys remain offline, attackers may compromise accounts or transaction workflows to initiate fraudulent withdrawal requests. Whether those requests can result in unauthorized transfers depends on the wallet architecture and the controls governing transaction approval and signing. Withdrawal restrictions,[transaction policies](https://www.bitgo.com/resources/blog/crypto-policy-engines/?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=custody&utm_campaign=best_practices_protecting_assets) , and independent approval requirements provide additional safeguards by controlling which transactions can be authorized and completed.


For more information about wallet types and custody arrangements, see BitGo's[wallet and custody guide](https://www.bitgo.com/resources/wallet-and-custody-guide/?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=custody&utm_campaign=best_practices_protecting_assets) .


## 2. Strengthen Account Authentication and Device Security


A secure wallet offers limited protection if an attacker can compromise the accounts or devices used to manage it. Cryptocurrency exchanges, wallet services, and email accounts are all potential entry points, making account security an essential part of protecting digital assets.


Strong, unique passwords help prevent a breach of one service from compromising other accounts. A reputable password manager can generate and store these credentials, while[multifactor authentication (MFA)](https://www.cisa.gov/secure-our-world/turn-mfa) adds another verification requirement beyond a password. Passkeys and hardware security keys that use phishing-resistant authentication can verify the website you're signing in to, making it harder for attackers to capture usable credentials through fake login pages.


Your primary email account deserves particular attention because it may be used to reset passwords or recover access to financial services. Securing that account helps protect the others connected to it.


Keep operating systems, browsers, and applications updated to address known vulnerabilities, and avoid installing software from unfamiliar sources. Be cautious of unexpected login pages or unfamiliar networks that could be used to steal credentials.


Wallet recovery phrases and private keys require additional care. Unlike ordinary account passwords, they may provide direct control over digital assets. Never share them with customer support representatives, enter them into unfamiliar websites, or store them in unsecured locations.


## 3. Recognize Phishing Attacks and Malicious Links


[Phishing attacks](https://www.cisa.gov/secure-our-world/recognize-and-report-phishing) use deceptive messages and websites to steal sensitive information or trick users into taking actions that compromise their accounts or wallets. In cryptocurrency, these attacks often impersonate exchanges, wallet providers, or other familiar services.


A fraudulent email might claim there's an urgent problem with your exchange account or offer a free token airdrop. Following the link could lead to a convincing imitation of a legitimate website designed to capture login credentials or recovery phrases. Attackers copy familiar branding, create lookalike domain names, and sometimes place fraudulent websites in[sponsored search results](https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2022/PSA221221) to make these schemes harder to recognize.


Other phishing attacks target wallet permissions rather than credentials. Fraudulent websites may encourage users to connect their wallets and then approve transactions or[grant permission to move tokens](https://www.chainalysis.com/blog/what-is-approval-phishing/) . Depending on the authorization granted, attackers may be able to transfer assets without obtaining the wallet's private keys.


Access cryptocurrency services through trusted bookmarks or independently verified website addresses, especially when responding to unexpected account alerts or security notifications.


Before connecting a wallet or signing a transaction, review what you're being asked to authorize. Requests for token spending permissions or unfamiliar approvals deserve particular scrutiny because they may grant access beyond a single intended transaction. Avoid proceeding when the purpose or scope of an authorization is unclear.


## 4. Independently Verify Unexpected Requests and Communications


Attackers may impersonate trusted organizations or individuals to convince cryptocurrency holders to disclose sensitive information, change account settings, or transfer digital assets.


These[impersonation scams](https://consumer.ftc.gov/features/how-avoid-imposter-scams) can occur through phone calls, emails, text messages, or social media. Someone claiming to represent a cryptocurrency exchange might warn that your account has been compromised and instruct you to transfer funds to a supposedly secure wallet.


Attackers can spoof phone numbers, imitate official communications, and use[AI-generated voices](https://www.bitgo.com/resources/blog/guarding-against-social-engineering-attacks/?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=custody&utm_campaign=best_practices_protecting_assets) to impersonate familiar people. They may also claim that funds will be lost unless you act immediately, leaving little time to question the request. Neither a recognizable voice nor an urgent warning is proof that the person contacting you is legitimate.


If someone unexpectedly contacts you about your account or assets, end the conversation and contact the organization through its official website or application. Never share passwords, recovery phrases, or authentication codes with an unexpected caller, and don't approve unfamiliar logins, disable security features, or transfer assets based solely on the caller's instructions.


## 5. Recognize Investment Scams and Fraudulent Opportunities


Not every cryptocurrency theft involves compromised accounts or malicious software. Some scams persuade victims to willingly transfer assets to fraudulent investments or trading platforms.


These schemes often begin on social media, dating platforms, or messaging applications. Scammers may pose as financial professionals, promote exclusive investment opportunities, or direct victims to websites that imitate legitimate trading services.


Some fraudulent platforms display fabricated account balances and investment returns to make victims believe their assets are growing. Scammers may even permit small withdrawals to establish credibility before encouraging larger deposits. When victims attempt to withdraw their funds, they may encounter unexpected fees, fabricated taxes, or demands for additional payments.


Promises of guaranteed returns, unusually high profits, or opportunities available only for a limited time are common warning signs. Cryptocurrency investments carry risk, and claims of consistent returns without the possibility of loss should be viewed skeptically.


Before transferring funds, independently research the investment opportunity rather than relying solely on advice from people encountered online, as recommended in the[FBI's guidance on cryptocurrency investment fraud](https://www.fbi.gov/how-we-can-help-you/victim-services/national-crimes-and-victim-resources/cryptocurrency-investment-fraud) . Verify the company's identity, confirm that you're using its legitimate website, and investigate claims about returns and withdrawals. Be especially cautious when someone you've never met directs you to an unfamiliar trading platform or wallet.


## Protect Your Digital Assets With BitGo


The principles behind protecting digital assets apply whether you're securing a personal wallet or managing assets for an institution. Secure storage, strong authentication, and careful[transaction authorization](https://www.bitgo.com/resources/blog/how-bitgo-is-redefining-transaction-security/?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=custody&utm_campaign=best_practices_protecting_assets) help reduce exposure to theft, while recognizing phishing and fraud remains essential to preventing losses.


For institutions, these protections must extend across the systems and workflows used to manage digital assets. BitGo brings together regulated custody, secure wallet infrastructure, and configurable[transaction policies](https://www.bitgo.com/resources/blog/crypto-policy-engines/?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=custody&utm_campaign=best_practices_protecting_assets) and approval workflows to help organizations safeguard assets and control how they are accessed and transferred.


From cold storage to[transaction authorization](https://www.bitgo.com/resources/blog/how-bitgo-is-redefining-transaction-security/?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=custody&utm_campaign=best_practices_protecting_assets) , BitGo provides the infrastructure institutions need to securely store, manage, and move digital assets.
